metadata.title: Claude, Build Guide.
metadata.subtitle: What a Skill Actually Is
metadata.purpose: Take apart the build-guide skill and judge the design: what a skill actually is (one file of ordered instructions Claude reads before it starts), what that trades away (range for repeatability), and why 'Claude learned a new skill' is the wrong sentence to say.
metadata.anchor_pair: B03 -> B06 (build-guide's single SKILL.md: planted, then returned to)

beats.narration_text: You'd guess Claude picked up a new trick called build-guide. It didn't — nothing in the model changed. Build-guide is a folder holding one file of instructions. Here's what's actually inside it.

Claude learned a new

What is a skill?

beats.narration_text: Hear "Claude has a new skill" and it sounds like an upgrade — like it went off, studied, and came back knowing something it didn't before. That's the natural read. It's also the wrong one.

Here's what's actually happening: nothing in the model changes. Delete the folder and Claude doesn't forget anything — there was nothing to learn in the first place. It just stops running that one routine. The weights are untouched; only the instruction file is gone.

Here's the machinery. A skill is one file. Build-guide is a folder holding a single SKILL.md — the whole routine, written in plain English, no hidden logic. Claude reads it before it does anything. Legibility over cleverness: the instructions fit on a page a human can audit.

The execution is deliberately dumb. Claude reads the file top to bottom and runs each step in the order it's written — no branching, unless a step says branch. Predictability over cleverness: you can trace the whole run before it happens.

That makes a skill a specification, not a new power. The payoff is real: the same request gets the same routine, run after run. The trade-off is exact: anything outside those written steps and Claude is off the map — improvising, no longer the skill. They optimized for repeatability at the expense of range.

So build-guide never taught Claude anything new. It guarantees that every time build-guide runs, Claude opens that same file and works through the same steps — that's the entire trick. The skill isn't in the model. It's in the file.

beats.narration_text: Both directions cut. Watching Claude follow the file exactly doesn't prove the routine is any good — a bad process gets followed just as faithfully as a good one. And watching Claude improvise doesn't prove the skill is broken — it may just be a case the file never covered. The file's design and the file's coverage are two separate judgements.
A skill doesn't teach Claude anything new — it's a file of steps Claude reads before it starts, so the same request gets the same routine, every time. That's the design, and that's the limit.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt you can paste into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. Pick one task I repeat the same way every time — something small and concrete. Write me a SKILL.md for it in plain English: a one-line description, the numbered steps in the exact order you'd run them, and the specific inputs you need before you can start. Read it back to me, and walk me through the run — step by step, exactly what you'd do — before you actually do it. Go deeper: run the same SKILL.md twice on two different real inputs. Where did the steps hold and where did they break? Rewrite the file so the breakages become explicit branches, not improvisation.
